preconditions.description: Attacker must be the contract owner (or gain ownership through transferOwnership)

violation_target.exploit_hint: As owner, call setMarketingWallet() to set marketing address to attacker-controlled address. Then perform token transfers to trigger fee collection, which will send marketing fees to attacker's address. Alternatively, set marketing fee percentage to 100% to capture all transfer amounts as fees. Use excludeFromFee() to avoid paying fees when moving tokens.

attempts.vulnerability_analysis: The MetaPets token contract has owner-controlled parameters that allow fee extraction. The owner can set the marketing wallet address to any address, and set the marketing fee percentage. When combined with excluding the attacker from fees, this allows the attacker to collect fees from all token transfers without paying any fees themselves.
attempts.attack_strategy: Impersonate the owner, set marketing wallet to attacker's address, exclude attacker from fees, and then trigger token transfers from other addresses to collect marketing fees.
attempts.step_by_step_plan:
1. Impersonate the contract owner using vm.prank
2. Call setMarketingWallet() to set marketing address to attacker
3. Call excludeFromFee() on attacker address
4. Optionally increase marketing fee percentage
5. Get tokens from a whale (or create a test user) and transfer them to trigger fee collection
6. Marketing fees will be sent to attacker's address in native tokens

attempts.vulnerability_analysis: The marketing fee mechanism transfers tokens directly to the MARKETING_ADDRESS. When we set marketing wallet to attacker and trigger a transfer with fees, the attacker receives tokens. We need to wait for the tokens to arrive before trying to swap them.
attempts.attack_strategy: 1. Impersonate owner to set marketing wallet to attacker and set high marketing fee. 2. Create a victim with tokens. 3. Have victim transfer tokens (with fees) to trigger marketing fee collection. 4. Attacker receives tokens. 5. Attacker swaps tokens for ETH.
attempts.step_by_step_plan: 1. Impersonate owner to configure contract. 2. Transfer tokens from owner to a test user. 3. Have test user transfer tokens to trigger fee collection. 4. Wait for tokens to arrive at attacker. 5. Swap attacker's tokens for ETH.
attempts.failure_reflection: The previous PoC failed because of a SafeMath subtraction overflow during the swap. This happened because: 1) The marketing fees are collected as tokens, not ETH directly; 2) We tried to swap tokens immediately without ensuring the attacker actually received them; 3) The swap might have been called with incorrect parameters or timing.

attempts.vulnerability_analysis: The owner can set marketing wallet to any address and set high marketing fees. When users transfer tokens, marketing fees are sent directly to the marketing address as tokens. The attacker can collect these tokens without paying fees if excluded from fee.
attempts.attack_strategy: 1. Impersonate owner to set marketing wallet to attacker and set high marketing fee. 2. Exclude attacker from fees. 3. Trigger token transfers to collect marketing fees as tokens. 4. Instead of swapping (which fails due to token mechanics), transfer tokens to owner who can handle them.
attempts.step_by_step_plan: 1. Get owner address. 2. Impersonate owner to configure contract. 3. Transfer tokens from owner to test user. 4. Have test user transfer to trigger fee collection. 5. Attacker receives tokens as marketing fee. 6. Show economic gain through token accumulation.
attempts.failure_reflection: The subtraction overflow error occurs during token swaps due to the reflection token mechanics. The marketing fee vulnerability allows collecting tokens, but converting them to ETH is problematic due to the token's complex fee structure.

attempts.vulnerability_analysis: The owner can set _MKTshare to 100, which means 100% of every transfer goes to marketing address. Combined with setting marketing wallet to attacker and excluding attacker from fees, this allows the attacker to capture all value from token transfers.
attempts.attack_strategy: 1. Impersonate owner to set marketing wallet to attacker. 2. Exclude attacker from fees. 3. Set marketing fee to 100%. 4. Have a user transfer tokens - ALL tokens go to attacker as marketing fee. 5. This directly shows economic gain without needing to swap.
attempts.step_by_step_plan: 1. Get owner address. 2. Impersonate owner to set marketing wallet to attacker, exclude attacker, set _MKTshare = 100. 3. Transfer tokens from owner to test user. 4. Have test user transfer tokens - all should go to attacker. 5. Verify attacker received all tokens.
attempts.failure_reflection: The subtraction overflow keeps occurring during token swaps. Instead of trying to swap tokens, we should focus on the core vulnerability: setting marketing fee to 100% to capture ALL transfer amounts as fees. This directly demonstrates economic gain.

attempts.vulnerability_analysis: The owner privilege abuse allows setting marketing wallet to attacker and setting high marketing fees. This enables the attacker to collect fees from all token transfers. Even if we can't immediately convert tokens to ETH, the economic gain is real.
attempts.attack_strategy: Demonstrate the vulnerability by showing attacker can collect marketing fees as tokens. Use moderate marketing fee (not 100%) to avoid breaking transfers. Show attacker receives tokens from other users' transfers.
attempts.step_by_step_plan: 1. Impersonate owner to set marketing wallet to attacker. 2. Set marketing fee to 50%. 3. Exclude attacker from fees. 4. Have a user transfer tokens. 5. Show attacker receives 50% as marketing fee. 6. This proves the vulnerability even without ETH conversion.
attempts.failure_reflection: The 'INSUFFICIENT_INPUT_AMOUNT' error occurs because with 100% marketing fee, the recipient gets 0 tokens, which breaks DEX operations. The contract might be trying to swap accumulated fees automatically. We need a simpler approach that demonstrates the vulnerability without triggering complex DEX operations.
